concepts.text: Article 29 — protection of interests of minorities

concepts.text: Article 32 — right to constitutional remedies
children: Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights
Dr. Ambedkar – most important article, soul of Constitution
Article 32 is a basic feature – cannot be abridged by amendment
Provisions: right to move SC guaranteed
SC can issue directions, orders, writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto)

Right to move SC cannot be suspended except during national emergency (Article 359)
Purpose – guaranteed, effective, expeditious, inexpensive, summary remedy
Only fundamental rights enforced under Article 32 – not other rights
Violation of fundamental right is sine qua non
SC cannot determine question not involving fundamental rights
Jurisdiction original but not exclusive – concurrent with High Court under Article 226
Alternate remedy no bar
SC ruled aggrieved should first move High Court if available

concepts.text: Writ of Habeas Corpus

Bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention
Issued against public authorities and private individuals
Not issued when detention lawful, contempt of legislature/court, detention by competent court, outside jurisdiction

concepts.text: Writ of Mandamus
children: Command to public official to perform duty – failed/refused
Against public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal, government
Not issued against private individual, departmental instruction without statutory force, discretionary duty, contractual obligation, President/governor, Chief Justice acting judicially

concepts.text: Writ of Prohibition
children: Higher court to lower court/tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction or usurping jurisdiction
Directs inactivity – unlike mandamus
Issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, not administrative, legislative, private

concepts.text: Writ of Certiorari
children: Higher court to lower court/tribunal to transfer case or quash order
Grounds: excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, error of law
Preventive and curative – unlike prohibition only preventive
Previously only against judicial/quasi-judicial; 1991 SC extended to administrative authorities affecting rights
Not available against legislative bodies and private individuals

concepts.text: Writ of Quo-Warranto

Prevents illegal usurpation of public office
Only for substantive public office of permanent character created by statute or Constitution – not ministerial or private office
Can be sought by any interested person, not necessarily aggrieved

concepts.text: Article 33 — power of Parliament to restrict/abrogate fundamental rights for armed forces, paramilitary, police, intelligence agencies, analogous forces

Power only with Parliament
Such law cannot be challenged in court
Army Act, 1950
Navy Act, 1950
Air Force Act, 1950
Police Forces (Restriction of Rights) Act, 1966

concepts.text: Article 34 — restrictions on fundamental rights while martial law in force

'Martial law' not defined in Constitution
Literally means military rule
Suspension of ordinary law and government by military tribunals

Imposed in extraordinary circumstances: war, invasion, insurrection, rebellion, riot, violent resistance to law

SC – declaration of martial law does not ipso facto suspend writ of habeas corpus

concepts.text: Differences between martial law and national emergency

Martial law suspends government and ordinary law courts; national emergency continues government and ordinary law courts
Martial law imposed to restore breakdown of law and order; national emergency imposed on three grounds: war, external aggression, armed rebellion
Martial law in specific area; national emergency in whole country or part
No specific provision in Constitution for martial law (implicit); detailed provision in Article 352 for national emergency (explicit)

concepts.text: Article 35 — legislation to give effect to certain fundamental rights
children: Power to make laws for specified matters vests only in Parliament

Restricting/abrogating FR for armed forces (Article 33)
Indemnifying during martial law (Article 34)
Power to prescribe punishment for offences under FR – untouchability (Article 17), traffic/forced labour (Article 23)
Mandatory for Parliament to enact such laws
Any law in force at commencement continues until altered/repealed/amended by Parliament
Article 35 extends Parliament's competence even if matter in State List

concepts.text: Right to property — original fundamental right and present position
children: Originally fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31
Article 19(1)(f) – right to acquire, hold, dispose of property (for citizens)
Article 31 – no person deprived of property except by authority of law; acquisition for public purpose with compensation
Most controversial fundamental right – confrontations between SC and Parliament
Constitutional amendments: 1st, 4th, 7th, 25th, 39th, 40th, 42nd
Articles 31A, 31B, 31C added and modified
44th Amendment 1978 – abolished right to property as FR, repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, inserted Article 300A in Part XII
Article 300A – no person deprived of property except by authority of law
Right to property remains legal/constitutional right, not fundamental
Not part of basic structure
Regulated by ordinary law – no constitutional amendment needed
Protects private property against executive action, not legislative action
Violation – cannot move SC under Article 32; can move HC under Article 226
No guaranteed compensation for acquisition/requisition

Two exceptions where compensation guaranteed in Part III: acquisition of minority educational institution property (Article 30); acquisition of land held under personal cultivation within statutory ceiling (Article 31A)

concepts.text: Article 31A — saving of laws for acquisition of estates, etc.
children: Saves five categories of laws from challenge under Articles 14 and 19: acquisition of estates and related rights; taking over management of properties by State; amalgamation of corporations; extinguishment/modification of rights of directors/shareholders; extinguishment/modification of mining leases
Law not immunised unless reserved for President's consideration and assent
Payment of compensation at market value for land under personal cultivation within ceiling

concepts.text: Article 31B — validation of certain acts and regulations in Ninth Schedule

Ninth Schedule – originally 13 acts, now (2016) 282

concepts.text: Article 31C — saving of laws giving effect to certain Directive Principles
children: Inserted by 25th Amendment 1971

Second provision: no law containing declaration that it gives effect to such policy questioned in court
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) – second provision declared unconstitutional (judicial review is basic feature)
First provision upheld as constitutional
42nd Amendment 1976 extended Article 31C protection to all directive principles – declared unconstitutional in Minerva Mills case (1980)

concepts.text: Criticism of Fundamental Rights
children: Excessive limitations
No social and economic rights (right to work, social security, rest, leisure)
Vague, indefinite, ambiguous language
No permanency – Parliament can curtail/abolish
Suspension during emergency (except Articles 20,21)
Expensive remedy – judicial process costly
Preventive detention (Article 22) negates liberty
No consistent philosophy – Sir Ivor Jennings called Constitution 'a paradise for lawyers'

concepts.text: Significance of Fundamental Rights
children: Bedrock of democratic system
Material and moral protection of man
Formidable bulwark of individual liberty
Establishment of rule of law
Protect interests of minorities and weaker sections
Strengthen secular fabric of Indian State
Check absoluteness of government authority
Foundation stone of social equality and social justice
Ensure dignity and respect of individuals
Facilitate participation in political and administrative process

concepts.text: Rights outside Part III (constitutional/legal rights, not fundamental)
children: Article 265 – no tax except by authority of law (Part XII)
Article 300-A – no person deprived of property save by authority of law (Part XII)
Article 301 – free trade, commerce and intercourse throughout territory (Part XIII)
Violation of non-fundamental right – cannot move SC under Article 32; can move HC by ordinary suit or under Article 226
